title: Adding and Subtracting Expressions
short: Subtracting an expression subtracts every term in it.
trouble: Students subtract only the first term of the second expression.

blocks.html: Adding and subtracting whole expressions uses two things you know: distributing a negative and combining like terms.
To add expressions, drop the parentheses and combine like terms. To subtract an expression, subtract every term in it: $-(cx + d) = -cx - d$. Then combine like terms.

Subtracting means adding the opposite, as with numbers. The opposite of a whole group is the opposite of each part: $-(x - 2)$ is $-1 \times (x - 2) = -x + 2$. If you took away only the $x$, you would have taken away less than the whole group.

head: Step
$(3x + 5) - (x - 2)$
rows: Write the subtraction as adding the opposite
blocks.cap: Subtracting a group, one step at a time.

blocks.html: Why does testing one number work as a check? Equivalent expressions are equal for every value of $x$. If your answer and the original give different values for $x = 1$, something went wrong. (Matching for one number is not a full proof, but it catches almost every slip.)

Subtracting only the first term: $(3x + 5) - (x - 2) = 2x + 3$. The $-2$ inside also gets subtracted, which turns it into $+2$. A quick check is to substitute a number, like $x = 1$, into the original and into your answer.
